title: Controllers and Actions
description: Learn how controllers handle HTTP requests in ASP.NET Core. Understand action methods, return types, action results, and how to use routing attributes to expose endpoints.

blocks.text: **Controllers** are the traffic cops of an ASP.NET Core MVC application. Every incoming HTTP request eventually reaches a controller action method. The controller decides what to do with the request — fetch data, update a record, or return an error — and then returns an appropriate response.

An **action** is simply a public method inside a controller class. Each action handles a specific type of request and returns an `IActionResult` (or a type that can be automatically converted to one).

A controller is a C# class that inherits from the `Controller` base class (for MVC) or `ControllerBase` (for APIs). The class name must end with `Controller` and is typically placed in the `Controllers/` folder.

blocks.title: A basic ProductsController
blocks.content: A simple MVC controller with two action methods for listing and displaying products.

blocks.text: Notice how each action method returns an `IActionResult`. This interface is the key to flexibility — it allows the controller to return different types of responses (HTML views, JSON, redirects, file downloads, error codes) all through the same return type.
ASP.NET Core provides many built-in action result types. Each one produces a different kind of HTTP response.

rows: You want to render an HTML view with a model
You want to return data as JSON (for APIs)
You want to send the user to another action
The requested resource does not exist
The request is malformed or invalid

blocks.title: Prefer specific return types in APIs
blocks.text: For API controllers, you can use the more specific return types like `ActionResult<Product>` or `IResult` instead of the generic `IActionResult`. This provides better API documentation and IntelliSense.
By default, ASP.NET Core uses a **convention-based route** defined in `Program.cs`. This default route maps URLs to controllers and actions using the pattern `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}`.

blocks.title: Default route pattern
blocks.content: The default route maps URL segments to controller, action, and optional id parameters.

blocks.text: With this route pattern, a URL like `/Products/Details/5` maps to `ProductsController.Details(5)`. The `id?` makes the `id` parameter optional, so `/Products` maps to `ProductsController.Index()` by default.

While convention-based routing works well for simple applications, **attribute routing** gives you full control by defining routes directly on controller actions using attributes. This is especially useful for APIs and complex URL structures.

blocks.title: Attribute routing on a controller
blocks.content: Use [Route] on the controller and [HttpGet] on actions to define custom URL patterns.

blocks.title: Route tokens
blocks.text: The `[controller]` token in route attributes is replaced with the controller name without the "Controller" suffix. So `[Route("[controller]")]` on `ProductsController` becomes `/products`. This keeps routes in sync with controller names automatically.

Action methods can be parameterless or accept parameters. ASP.NET Core's model binding automatically populates action parameters from the incoming HTTP request — from the URL route, query string, form data, or request body.

blocks.title: Action with multiple parameters
blocks.content: Parameters are automatically bound from the route, query string, and form data.

blocks.text: You can restrict which HTTP methods an action responds to using attributes. This is a form of method-level routing that ensures an action only handles the correct verb.

blocks.title: HTTP method attributes
items: **[HttpGet]** — Responds to GET requests (page loads, API reads)
**[HttpPost]** — Responds to POST requests (form submissions, API creates)
**[AcceptVerbs("GET", "POST")]** — Responds to multiple specified HTTP methods

terms.definition: A C# class that inherits from Controller and groups related action methods. Controllers handle incoming HTTP requests for a specific area of the application.
A public method inside a controller that handles a specific HTTP request and returns an IActionResult.
An interface representing the result of an action method. It allows controllers to return different response types (views, JSON, redirects, errors) through a common interface.
Defining routes directly on controllers and actions using attributes like [Route] and [HttpGet], rather than relying on convention-based routing.
The automatic process of populating action method parameters from the incoming HTTP request (route data, query string, form data, or request body).

blocks.title: Build a ProductsController with Multiple Actions
blocks.description: Create a ProductsController with actions for listing all products, viewing a single product, and displaying products by category.
steps: Create a new file `Controllers/ProductsController.cs` in your project
Add a class `ProductsController` that inherits from `Controller`
Add a static list of product strings as simulated data: Laptop, Coffee Mug, Desk Lamp, Notebook, Headphones
Create an `Index()` action that returns all products to a view
Create a `Details(int id)` action that returns a single product by ID, or `NotFound()` if the ID is out of range
Create a `ByCategory(string category)` action that filters products (hint: use a simple string check)
Run the app and navigate to `/Products`, `/Products/Details/2`, and `/Products/ByCategory?category=Electronics`
blocks.expectedOutcome: Visiting `/Products` shows a list of products. `/Products/Details/2` shows the product at index 2. Navigating to an invalid ID like `/Products/Details/99` shows a 404 Not Found response.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Controllers are C# classes that group related HTTP request handlers
Action methods are public methods that return IActionResult
Common action results include View(), Json(), RedirectToAction(), NotFound(), BadRequest()
Convention-based routing maps URLs to controllers automatically using the {controller}/{action}/{id?} pattern
Attribute routing lets you define custom URL patterns directly on actions with [Route] and [HttpGet]
Model binding automatically populates action parameters from the request
blocks.takeaway: Controllers and actions are the central mechanism for handling HTTP requests in ASP.NET Core. Mastering action methods, return types, and routing attributes gives you full control over how your application responds to every URL.
